title: Master Class | Oh My Cheaters!! | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: The Nimzowitsch-Larsen — b3 and the bishop to b2. It's a hypermodern opening: instead of building our own center, we attack the opponent's from a distance with our pieces.
e3 is the old main line — pure hypermodern, with all our pressure aimed at the enemy center rather than our own.
The bishop to b5 hits the knight and threatens to win the e5-pawn.
The queen to e7 defends, but at a real cost — it makes Black's kingside bishop much harder to develop.
teaches: Qe7 defends but blocks his own development

moves.spoken: The knight goes to e2, not f3 — f3 would invite ...e4 with tempo, and we want to leave that pawn on the operating table. The e2 square also prepares a second plan.
We take the knight. Even though e5 is no longer attacked directly, we can pile straight back onto it — Black is already in trouble just six moves in.
The pawn to f4 pries at e5 — d4 would only block in our own bishop and hand Black the ...e4 push.
teaches: f4, not d4, to open the bishop and hit e5

moves.spoken: The knight takes the awkward route — first to a3, the Frankfurt airport, on its way toward the center.
teaches: reroute via the rim toward the center

moves.spoken: Then to c4 — ugly, but imagine how good it'll look once it reaches e5. No rush, though: the threat is stronger than its execution.
teaches: the threat is stronger than the execution

moves.spoken: Black castles long — so we have opposite-side castling, a straight race of attacks.
Our attack starts with a4, heading for b4 and b5 to blast open his queenside pawn cover — and in opposite-side castling you simply have to get on with it.
teaches: a4-b4-b5 to crack the castled king
